To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the consumer is the main actor in this article and the main actor has been involved in a number of activities that have been beneficial to the consumer.

the modernization of the health care system in Britain and Germany has been characterized by different inflections of consumerism, different forms of consumer participation and, as a result, different implications for the role of the state in the governance of the health care sector.

(1) the consumer has entered the political stage; (2) this has happened through a process of modernization of health services in which the consumer has been given more information and more power; (3) this process is different in Britain and Germany; (4) the different inflections of consumerism in Britain and Germany are associated with their different institutional histories and their different current political projects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which consumer participation in the governance of health care is being reconfigured in the context of modernization.
the ways in which consumerist ideas and practices are being refracted through the institutional histories and current projects of different health systems.
the political implications of consumer involvement in the modernization of the welfare state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the consumer is not a new player in the health system.
the modernization of European health care systems has been associated with the emergence of new forms of consumerism, but that these are highly variable and contextually specific.
consumerism is a political project that is refracted through the institutional and cultural histories of health care systems and the current political projects of reforming them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the modernization of European health systems involves new governance practices which seek to equip citizens with the power to make choices about health care and to involve them as `stakeholder' in health systems.
consumerism in health care is not a simple process but one that is mediated by institutional and cultural contexts.
the consumer is not an abstract entity that can be inserted into health care in the same way across countries, and that the meaning of consumer empowerment in health care is not a fixed concept.
The main takeaway from our work is that
consumer involvement in health care systems is not a simple, linear process of increasing consumer choice.
consumer involvement is not a straightforward matter of `giving power' to consumers.
consumer involvement is not simply about the empowerment of patients.
